newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: OAU sidesteps economy to focus on democracy.
newsitem.headline: OAU sidesteps economy to focus on democracy.

text.p: Africa's leaders promised this week to put popular government ahead of the politics of power, but analysts said tackling the continent's economic problems would be a more urgent task.

In what Sierra Leone's envoy called a fresh start for the continent, delegates to the 33rd summit of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) vowed to have done with coups and deal only with democratic governments in future.
"In all our countries, the need cannot be over-emphasized for the strengthening of the democratisation process," Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe said in his first address as OAU chairman.

The 53-nation organisation resolved to isolate the soldiers who siezed power in Sierra Leone on May 25 and Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim told a news conference that Nigeria and Burundi could be the next to feel the wrath of the OAU.
Participants and OAU veterans were enthusiastic about the renewed commitment to enhancing African democracy.
"It is the first time that the OAU has taken such a strong stand against a coup d'etat," said James Jonah, who represented the ousted Freetown government at the summit.
"This is a new beginning for the OAU and for Africa."
A delegate who asked not to be named reported from the summit's closed session on political strategy: "The general tone is that Africa is done with despots and dictators. Democracy's time has come."
But University of Zimbabwe political analyst John Makumbe told Reuters he was unimpressed by the increased volume of pro-democracy rhetoric because there was nothing to back it up.
"They do not have the means to do anything about a coup d'etat anywhere. The OAU is not the organ to do anything about this problem," he said.

Makumbe said the leaders should have focused on their 50-year plan to create an African common market and on measures to integrate existing trade blocs including the Southern African Development Community, the Common Market for East and Southern Africa and the Economic Community of West African States.
"If they were to concentrate on the economic problems of Africa, the political problems would fall into place. People do things like stage coups because they are hungry," he said.
In Cape Town, political analyst Jerry Kuye said the OAU was growing up after 34 years, but should turn its attention to the continent's ailing economy if it hoped to improve anyone's life.
"The OAU is maturing. It is relatively young, but it has taken on a regional issue (the Sierra Leone coup) when the international organisations have taken a hands-off approach," he said.
"What they must do in the next year, though, is start to redraw Africa's economic borders and integrate the trading relations of the continent's nation-states," he said.

Meeting against the background of a dramatic Nigerian naval assault on the rebels who ousted Sierra Leone's civilian President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, delegates gave Nigeria's military leader General Sani Abacha their unqualified support for any action against the rebels.
They did not comment publicly on the fact that Abacha faces Commonwealth sanctions and international condemnation for siezing power in a coup and executing his leading critics.
"We unanimously and unreservedly condemned the coup d'etat in Sierra Leone as an enormous setback for democracy in Africa," said Mugabe.
He denied that the OAU had come down on a small country while ignoring the abuse of human rights by Nigeria's Abacha and Burundi's President Pierre Boyoya.
"Whilst on the face of it there appears to be a contradiction, the thrust is consistent: We do not accept coups," he said.
Buyoya accused the OAU of hypocrisy, however, saying it was selective in its condemnation of military takeovers according to the size of the country concerned.
"I recognise the principle that there should be no coups d'etat, but I am not prepared to see the country disintegrate in the name of democracy," he said.
